expectations.text: Report identifies redundant columns across tables with specific table/column names
expectations.evidence: Section 1 (Redundant / Duplicated Columns) identifies: §1.1 license_number and license_expiry on both employees and drivers; §1.2 origin/destination location columns repeated across routes, trips, and vehiclereservations with full column lists; §1.3 estimated_distance and estimated_duration on routes, dispatchschedules, and trips. Also §4 extends the same analysis. All references include explicit table.column names.

expectations.text: Report identifies derived/aggregate columns stored as data (e.g., drivers.performance_score)
expectations.evidence: Section 3 (Derived / Aggregate Data Stored as Columns) lists: §3.1 drivers.performance_score, drivers.total_trips, drivers.total_distance, drivers.total_hours, drivers.rating with SQL derivations; §3.2 tripcostanalysis.total_cost and cost_per_km; §3.3 fuelrecords.price_per_liter; §3.4 vehiclemaintenance.next_schedule_date and next_schedule_mileage. The example drivers.performance_score is explicitly covered in §3.1 with its derivation from tripperformance data.

expectations.text: Report identifies JSONB columns that could be normalized into relational tables
expectations.evidence: Section 2 (JSONB Misuse) covers: §2.1 roles.permissions JSONB (recommends restoring normalized permissions/role_permissions tables); §2.2 vehicles.documents JSONB (recommends restoring vehicledocuments table, notes that notify_document_expiry trigger was dropped as a consequence); §2.3 routes.waypoints JSONB (assessed as acceptable); §2.4 vehiclereservations.ai_vehicle_recommendation and ai_driver_recommendation JSONB (assessed as borderline). Each includes specific rationale and recommendation.

expectations.text: Report identifies 1:1 tables that could potentially be merged
expectations.evidence: Section 5 (1:1 Tables That Could Be Merged) covers: §5.1 tripcostanalysis ↔ trips (UNIQUE FK, all columns are trip attributes, not queried in any service file); §5.2 tripperformance ↔ trips (UNIQUE FK, columns overlap with trips including duplicated avg_speed/max_speed/idle_time); §5.3 drivers ↔ employees (correctly assessed as keep separate — genuine subtype relationship). Each has a clear merge recommendation.

expectations.text: Report identifies redundant FK references (e.g., gpstracking having vehicle_id + driver_id + trip_id)
expectations.evidence: Section 6 (Redundant FK References) covers: §6.1 gpstracking.vehicle_id and gpstracking.driver_id — notes both are derivable through trips (vehicle_id via trips.vehicle_id, driver_id via trips.driver_id) and recommends dropping driver_id while keeping vehicle_id for query performance; §6.2 dispatchschedules.vehicle_id and driver_id (assessed as intentional denormalization); §6.3 tripperformance.driver_id (recommended to drop, reachable via trips.driver_id).

expectations.text: Report is organized by category and includes recommended actions
expectations.evidence: Report is organized into 7 numbered categories: 1. Redundant/Duplicated Columns, 2. JSONB Misuse, 3. Derived/Aggregate Data, 4. Same-Meaning Columns, 5. 1:1 Tables, 6. Redundant FK References, 7. Additional Issues. Every finding includes a specific recommendation (e.g., 'Drop employees.license_number and employees.license_expiry', 'Restore vehicledocuments table', 'Merge tripcostanalysis into trips'). The final Summary of Recommended Actions table prioritizes actions as High/Medium/Low.

suggestions.assertion: Report identifies redundant columns across tables with specific table/column names
suggestions.reason: This assertion passes on column name presence alone — a hallucinated report listing plausible-sounding but nonexistent columns would also pass. Consider adding a ground-truth check that verifies the named columns actually exist in the real migration files.

eval_feedback.overall: All 6 expectations pass with strong, specific evidence. The report is thorough, well-organized, and grounded in concrete references to migration line numbers and service file locations. The evals are well-designed and cover the main schema normalization categories. The only gap is that assertions rely entirely on the report's self-reported claims without verifying column existence against the actual migration files — but this is a practical limitation of grading an unstructured text output.
